hints: Focus on what is different about this benzene, the double bonds are frozen in one place and cannot move around the ring.
Fix one Cl on a carbon, then think about the second Cl in ortho positions next door, one neighbour is joined by a double bond and the other by a single bond.
Check the meta and para positions too, then add up how many truly different surroundings exist for the pair of Cl atoms.
walkthrough:
**Recall the real benzene result**

In real benzene all C-C bonds are identical because of delocalisation. So dichlorobenzene has only 3 isomers: 1,2-ortho, 1,3-meta and 1,4-para.

$$\text{real benzene} \rightarrow 3 \text{ isomers}$$

**See what freezing the Kekule bonds changes**

Here the double bonds are fixed as shown: three alternating $C=C$ and three $C-C$. That means two carbons joined by $C=C$ are in a different environment from two carbons joined by $C-C$.

$$C=C \text{ is different from } C-C$$

**Split the ortho isomer into two**

Put the first $Cl$ on carbon 1. Its two adjacent neighbours are not the same. One neighbour is joined to it by a double bond, the other neighbour is joined by a single bond. Rotation cannot turn one into the other without moving the double bonds.

$$\text{ortho (adjacent) } \rightarrow 2 \text{ isomers: } Cl-C= C-Cl \text{ and } Cl-C-C-Cl$$

**Check meta and para**

For meta, 1,3 and 1,5 arrangements, rotation plus reflection of the whole fixed skeleton makes them superimposable, so there is only 1 meta type. For para, 1,4 opposite, there is only 1 type.

$$\text{meta} \rightarrow 1, \quad \text{para} \rightarrow 1$$

**Add them up**

Total distinct $C_6H_4Cl_2$ structures = 2 ortho + 1 meta + 1 para = 4.

$$2 + 1 + 1 = 4$$

options.A: 3 is the number for real delocalised benzene with ortho, meta and para only. It ignores the question condition that double bonds stay fixed, which splits ortho into two different isomers.
options.B: 4 is correct: 2 different ortho forms (Cl atoms separated by a double bond versus by a single bond) plus 1 meta form plus 1 para form. Freezing the Kekule structure removes the equivalence of the two ortho neighbours.
options.C: 5 is too many. It comes from counting both ortho as two and both meta as two (1,3 and 1,5 as different). In fact the two meta-like pairs are superimposable by rotating the whole molecule with its fixed double bonds, so they are the same isomer.
options.D: 6 is too many. It comes from thinking every second Cl position 2,3,4,5,6 gives a new isomer with Cl at position 1. Symmetry still makes some positions equivalent, leaving only 4 distinct pairs.
